subject: religious-studies
title: The Creedal Chamber: Trinity and Incarnation
welcome_lead: Enter the council chamber of Nicaea and Chalcedon, where the central doctrines of Christianity were hammered into creeds.
meta_desc: A-Level Religious Studies adventure on the Trinity and the Incarnation in Christian doctrine.
final_note: The creeds are not philosophy but worship struggling to be precise.

concepts.def: The Christian doctrine that God is one substance (ousia) in three persons (hypostases): Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
The doctrine that the eternal Son of God became fully human in Jesus Christ without ceasing to be divine.
'Of one substance'; the term used at Nicaea (325) to affirm that the Son shares the same divine substance as the Father.
The Chalcedonian definition (451) that Christ is one person in two natures, divine and human, 'without confusion or change'.
The Latin clause 'and from the Son', added to the Nicene Creed in the West to affirm the Spirit's procession from both Father and Son.
The mutual indwelling or 'dance' of the three persons of the Trinity, expressing their unity in distinction.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Called by Emperor Constantine to address the Arian controversy, the First Council of Nicaea (325) affirmed that the Son is homoousios with the Father, against Arius' claim that there was a time when the Son was not.

The Nicene Creed (in its expanded 381 form) remains the most widely used statement of Trinitarian faith.

The Council of Chalcedon defined that the one person Jesus Christ exists 'in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation'.

This 'hypostatic union' guards against both Nestorianism (which separated the natures into two persons) and Eutychianism / Monophysitism (which fused them into one).

Augustine's De Trinitate (c. 400) developed a 'psychological analogy': memory, understanding, and will mirror Father, Son, and Spirit in the human soul.

The Cappadocian Fathers (Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus, Gregory of Nyssa) emphasised the three persons sharing one essence, with perichoresis describing their mutual indwelling.

mcqs.q: Which Greek term affirms that the Son shares the Father's substance?
options: Homoousios
Homoiousios
Perichoresis
Hypostasis

mcqs.q: Chalcedon (451) is best known for defining which doctrine?
options: The hypostatic union
The procession of the Spirit
The canon of Scripture
Papal primacy

mcqs.q: What is the doctrine of the Trinity?
options: Christians believe in three different gods.
Jesus was a human who became God after his resurrection.
God is one being existing in three persons (Father, Son, Holy Spirit) — distinct in person but united in essence; Christians remain monotheistic.
The Trinity refers to heaven, earth and hell.
Aquinas's Five Ways are five steps of one cosmological argument.

Five distinct arguments for God's existence: from motion, causation, contingency, gradation of being, and final causes/teleology — collectively forming Aquinas's natural theology, not a single argument.
Jesus was a human who became God after his resurrection.
Aquinas's Five Ways are five Christian sacraments.

mcqs.q: What do orthodox Christians believe about the nature of Jesus?
options: Jesus was half God and half human.
He is fully God and fully human at the same time (the incarnation) — both natures united in one person, as defined at the Council of Chalcedon.
Jesus was a human who became God after his resurrection.
The Trinity refers to heaven, earth and hell.

mcqs.q: In what year did the First Council of Nicaea take place?
Apollinarianism was condemned because it denied that Christ had:
options: a full human mind or rational soul
a real physical body
any divine nature
the same substance as the Father

mcqs.q: Kenosis, drawn from Philippians 2:7, refers to:
options: the Son's self-emptying in becoming human
the procession of the Spirit from the Father
the mutual indwelling of the three persons
the resurrection of the body

mcqs.q: The Council of Constantinople (381) is particularly significant for:
options: affirming the divinity of the Holy Spirit and expanding the Nicene Creed
defining the two natures of Christ in one person
condemning the use of icons
settling the date of Easter permanently

mcqs.q: The Chalcedonian Definition's four adverbs — 'without confusion, change, division, separation' — function to:
options: set boundaries on how the two natures relate, without explaining the mechanism of their union
explain precisely how divinity and humanity combine
deny that Christ had two natures
affirm that the union began at the resurrection
